Stocks are significantly outperforming housing over the US over the long run:

Since 1975, the S&P 500 has delivered an average annual total return of +12.2%. 

This is more than double the +5.1% annual gain in US home prices over the same period.

Even without reinvesting dividends, the S&P 500 has still returned an average of +9.3% per year, outperforming house price appreciation.

After adjusting for inflation, the gap is even wider, with the S&P 500's real total return at +8.3% over the last 50 years, nearly 6 times the +1.4% real annual return of US home prices.

At the same time, the S&P 500 excluding dividends and adjusted for inflation has returned +5.4% per year, on average.

Stocks have been a far more powerful driver of wealth creation than housing.

The surge was driven by investors buying the dip and banks increasing gold imports to rebuild inventories amid strong retail demand.

Meanwhile, gold-backed ETFs in China have attracted +28 tonnes of inflows year-to-date.

China's appetite for gold is incredibly strong.

China’s economy is built on an extraordinary savings surplus:

China’s gross national savings rate stands at ~43% of GDP, the highest among the world’s largest economic blocs.

This is more than double the US' rate of ~18%.

China’s savings rate has remained above 40% for nearly the entire century while the US has not exceeded 20% over the same period.

Meanwhile, Japan’s savings rate is ~32% of GDP, while the Eurozone’s is ~24%, both well below China.

A high savings rate provides a larger pool of domestic capital that can be used to finance investment, expand manufacturing capacity, and strengthen its industrial base.

China’s savings surplus is a powerful source of investment capacity.

Americans are sitting on a record $8 trillion in cash.

That is the fuel under every dip. This much cash is not going to sit still for very long.

tweets.text: On this day in 1909, French aviator Louis Blériot flew a fragile 25-horsepower monoplane across the English Channel in about 37 minutes, becoming the first person to cross a major body of water by airplane and winning a £1,000 prize put up by the Daily Mail newspaper. Blériot had crashed and rebuilt his aircraft dozens of times, sinking most of a fortune he had earned manufacturing acetylene headlamps for automobiles into his flying machines. The crossing turned him into a celebrity and a businessman overnight: orders for his Blériot XI poured in, and he sold more than 100 of them within months, building one of the world's first successful aircraft companies. The flight also shattered Britain's sense of security as an island and spurred a surge in military spending on air power. The global aviation industry that day's flight helped launch now generates over $800 billion a year.

Blériot had crashed and rebuilt his aircraft dozens of times, sinking most of a fortune he had earned manufacturing acetylene headlamps for automobiles into his flying machines. The crossing turned him into a celebrity and a businessman overnight: orders for his Blériot XI poured in, and he sold more than 100 of them within months, building one of the world's first successful aircraft companies. The flight also shattered Britain's sense of security as an island and spurred a surge in military spending on air power. The global aviation industry that day's flight helped launch now generates over $800 billion a year.

thread_tweets.text:
They’re massive. I’m going to give my analysis in a tweet? The answer to almost everything in them is: run the implementation you want.

Here’s a specific: Some argue that bitcoin *needs* non-monetary data to sure up the long-term fee market, and that view came up in the articles. I don’t believe bitcoin needs those fees, and I think fees from monetary demand are sufficient. If bitcoin can’t secure itself from monetary fees decades out, then that’s a big lack of demand for bitcoin as money, not something that JPEGs on the timechain will fix. I do not support changes to bitcoin for the purpose of adding more non-monetary fees, and I disagree with the arguments that bitcoin needs to be more expressive to survive (this was a big topic in 2024 when we wrote BCAP).

I’m happy that things like open timestamps exist (lets anyone prove that something was unaltered, referenced to the near-immutability of bitcoin), and fortunately that has basically infinite information density and doesn’t fill up blocks or put bad content into the chain itself. So there are these tiny non-monetary use cases that are interesting, but they don’t need almost any accommodation to work.
